title: Why Anthropic's Record IPO Lost Half Its Pop

items.text: This is the moment Anthropic became the biggest IPO in history.
The maker of Claude raised 93.5 billion dollars, more than any company had ever raised in a stock market debut.
Its shares opened at 111 dollars and 50 cents, 34 percent above the price set the night before.
And one day later, more than half of that first-day gain was gone.
So what happened? Let's go back to the start.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven people who left OpenAI.
Dario Amodei became chief executive. His sister Daniela became president.
The other five co-founders are Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Chris Olah.
Their company makes Claude, a family of AI models that first launched in 2023.
And Claude has grown fast. In the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic's revenue was 33.24 billion dollars, about 13 times as much as a year earlier.
In the third quarter alone, it was about 17 billion dollars.

On paper, it still lost 104 billion dollars in those nine months. But most of that was an accounting charge: its convertible notes became worth more as the company did. The business itself lost about 1.3 billion dollars.
At Nasdaq, Daniela Amodei put it bluntly.
Part of that is written into its legal structure. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation.
By law, it has to weigh its shareholders against its mission: the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.
Even after the listing, the seven co-founders keep 50.1 percent of the votes, through a special entity called Founder LLC.
That matters, because from now on outside shareholders own most of the company.
On the 10th of November, Anthropic started its roadshow, the meetings where the banks pitch a new stock to big investors.
The plan was to sell 825 million shares at 70 to 78 dollars each.
But demand was so strong that the plan changed.
On the 18th of November, Anthropic priced its shares at 83 dollars, above the top of the range.
And instead of 825 million shares, it sold 980 million.
Raising the price and the number of shares at the same time is a clear sign that the banks had far more orders than shares to sell.
That first sale alone was worth 81.3 billion dollars.
The next morning, the shares would start trading on Nasdaq, under the ticker ANT.
On Thursday the 19th of November, the Nasdaq tower in Times Square was covered in Anthropic's imagery.
Down at street level, New York went about its morning.
Inside the MarketSite studio, Nasdaq's chair and chief executive, Adena Friedman, opened the ceremony.
Then Daniela Amodei took the podium.
She said more than half of the Fortune 500 now use Claude.
And she described what the company wants Claude to be.
Next came her brother, Dario Amodei.
He started with medicine, and with a big claim.
Then he turned to the risks of AI, and made a promise that investors will remember.
For a company that just sold shares to the public, that is an unusual thing to say on day one.
He closed with the line that Nasdaq later quoted in its own release.
Then the whole team walked up for the bell.
The bell rang, and Anthropic was a public company!
But the bell does not start trading in a brand new stock. The first trade in ANT only came just before noon.
And when it came, it was 111 dollars and 50 cents, 34 percent above the IPO price!
At that price, Anthropic was worth around 2 trillion dollars, fully diluted.
Fully diluted means you also count the stock the company has promised to employees, but has not handed out yet.
Counting only the shares that already exist, the value was about 1.5 trillion dollars. Still one of the most valuable companies in America, on its first morning.
So how big was this sale, really?
On the first day, the 980 million shares brought in 81.3 billion dollars.
On Friday, the banks used their option to buy 147 million extra shares, a step known as the greenshoe.
Banks normally only use that option when a new stock trades above its IPO price. And ANT did.
That lifted the total to 93.5 billion dollars.
SpaceX, the previous record holder, raised 75 billion dollars in June, and 85.7 billion with its own extra shares.
So, counted the same way, Anthropic is the new record.
And there was more. Seven technology companies bought another 26 billion dollars of a separate class of shares, at the same 83 dollars.
Together, the offering and that private sale add up to 119.5 billion dollars.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led the deal.
So who owns Anthropic now?
Amazon owns about 14.7 percent and Google about 13.7 percent.
Both are also major suppliers of the computing power that Anthropic runs on.
The seven co-founders each hold about 240 million shares, together about 10 percent of the company.
At the IPO price, that is roughly 20 billion dollars per founder.
And Reuters expects the listing to create thousands of paper millionaires among the staff.
Unusually, employees were allowed to sell up to 10 percent of their shares on the very first day. Most companies make their staff wait for months.
But on the trading floor, the price was already sliding.
After that opening trade, buyers who got in at 83 dollars locked in quick profits through the afternoon.
At four o'clock, Anthropic was back at Nasdaq for the closing bell.
This time chief commercial officer Paul Smith and chief financial officer Krishna Rao spoke, with some of Anthropic's customers on stage.
ANT closed its first day at 97 dollars and 17 cents.
That is still 17 percent above the IPO price. A strong first day by any normal standard.
And here is the uncomfortable side of a big first-day pop. Every share Anthropic sold at 83 dollars was worth 97 dollars by the evening.
On 980 million shares, that is roughly 14 billion dollars that went to the first buyers instead of to the company.
Fully diluted, Anthropic was now worth about 1.8 trillion dollars.
Then came Friday.
The AI trade was already nervous. Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang had just left the company, and investors were asking whether all the spending on AI would pay off.
On Friday, that fear boiled over. Nvidia fell about 14 percent, and AMD lost about 13 percent. Amazon, Google and Microsoft closed lower too.
Anthropic could not escape it. ANT fell 8.5 percent, to 88 dollars and 91 cents, close to its 83 dollar IPO price.
More than half of the first-day gain was gone in a single session.
Does that make the IPO a failure? Not for Anthropic.
The company got its money at 83 dollars a share, whatever the stock does next.
The record itself is safe for now. Remember, SpaceX held it for only five months.
And as the first frontier AI lab on the stock market, it has no direct peer to be measured against.
From now on, every quarter, ANT will show whether investors still believe in the AI boom.
So what do you think? Is this the start of something huge, or the top of the AI bubble? Tell me in the comments.
